source.title: Scaling Laws of Motion Forecasting and Planning - A Technical Report
source.authors: Mustafa Baniodeh; Kratarth Goel; Scott Ettinger; Carlos Fuertes; Ari Seff; Tim Shen; Cole Gulino; Chenjie Yang; Ghassen Jerfel; Dokook Choe; Rui Wang; Benjamin Charrow; V. Kallem; Sergio Casas; Rami Al-Rfou; Benjamin Sapp; D. Anguelov

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling laws for motion forecasting and planning, a non-language generative task, and reports compute-optimal allocation and downstream metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own scaling, downstream-evaluation, closed-loop, and cross-agent-transfer results. It also discusses language-model scaling laws, but cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains 84 encoder-decoder motion-forecasting transformers (0.9M–118M parameters) over seven compute budgets spanning about two orders of magnitude. It runs its own iso-FLOP analysis and reports loss, compute-optimal allocation, open- and closed-loop metric scaling, and cross-agent transfer. This is a new, non-text setting with its own results, so it bears mainly on V5 and, setting-limited, on V3, V6 and V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right but incomplete. The authors conclude that cross-entropy improves as a power law (better fit with a constant) when model and data are scaled with compute. Optimal model size should grow about 1.5× as fast as data, and optimal models are about 50× smaller than LLMs at equal compute. Open- and closed-loop metrics improve with scale, though the compute range cannot establish power laws for them. Inference sampling helps smaller models up to a crossover point. Training on other agents transfers zero-shot to the AV.
record.recipe_differences: Uses iso-FLOP analysis associated with Hoffmann et al., but applies it to encoder-decoder motion-forecasting models and training examples rather than decoder-only language models and tokens.

fits_no_version.finding: At the same compute, optimal motion-forecasting models are about 50× smaller than LLMs. The allocation split (model grows ~1.5× as fast as data) matches neither Kaplan nor Hoffmann.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal model/data split depends on data domain or modality.

fits_no_version.finding: Ten miles observed from other agents are worth 2–3 ego-demonstrated miles at matched AV loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-agent data transfers to the ego agent at a fixed exchange rate.

fits_no_version.finding: Inference-time sampling (8–1024 samples) improves minADE, minFDE and mAP up to a crossover point, beyond which a larger model is more inference-efficient.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-compute scaling trades off against model size.

record.problems: The principal compute sweep spans more than two orders of magnitude, and the authors say the observed curvature may be near an irreducible term or arise from dataset and interface factors. They caution that the open-loop distance-metric study lacks the compute range and statistical methodology needed to establish a scaling law. Numerical values for several agent-specific fits and evaluation curves are presented in figures rather than stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the listed versions were left out.

untested.parts: No language models were trained; held-out loss scaling is shown only for motion forecasting.
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs.
Layers vary at a fixed width-to-depth ratio (8 or 16). Shapes are not compared at fixed parameter count.
Language models and token-count allocation are not tested.
Image and video models, repeated-data scaling and conventional fine-tuning or transfer scaling are not tested.
Language-model downstream benchmarks are not tested; only driving metrics are.

missing.what: Optimal model sizes chosen by minADE differ from those chosen by cross-entropy at low compute (smaller), and are consistent at high compute. The optimum depends on the evaluation metric.
Inference-scaling results for three models: minADE, minFDE, miss rate and mAP versus number of samples, with crossover points.
Discussion statement that cross-entropy and all metrics are better explained by a power law plus constant.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its settings are outside text, so the V3 and V6 verdicts are limited to motion forecasting. I dropped the reader's V5 limits_scope label on R1, because a power law plus constant is the standard form for non-text modalities; the curvature is credited to V7 instead. Per-agent exponents appear only in figures.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments use motion forecasting models, not language models.
The paper does not report testing whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.
Tests optimal parameter count and training-example count against compute in this motion-forecasting setup, not language models or token counts.
The model-size sweep varies encoder and decoder layers while keeping width-to-depth ratio at either 8 or 16; it does not compare architecture shapes at fixed parameter count.
Tests motion forecasting, including cross-agent transfer, but not image or video models, repeated-data training, or fine-tuning and transfer across conventional downstream tasks.
Tests open-loop distance metrics and one closed-loop simulation metric; other downstream tasks are not tested.
Reports curvature and better fit from adding a constant, but does not systematically vary parameter counting, schedule, data, or fitting method to measure their effects on exponents or allocation.

rows.subject: Encoder-decoder transformer models (compute-optimal models)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size, training examples, and training compute; extracted optimal loss from iso-FLOP bands.

conditions.value: 541 million training examples; 447 thousand hours of driving
seven compute budgets spanning more than two orders of magnitude

rows.measure: Compute-optimal validation cross-entropy loss as a function of training compute
rows.value: The loss improves as a power law; adding a constant captures the curvature significantly better.
rows.uncertainty: 3 standard deviations propagated from fit-parameter covariance are shown in the figure.
rows.note: The authors say the data points curve and may be close to an irreducible term; they identify limited data, repeated passes, overlapping examples, data mixture, and perception inputs as possible contributors.
rows.check: For V5 the state should be observed: the loss follows a power law plus constant, the same form Henighan et al. report for other modalities. For V7 the curvature away from a pure power law is also observed. The reader's 'partial' mixes the two versions.

rows.uncertainty: ±0.08 in the exponent; 3-standard-deviation error bars and propagated fit bands are described.
rows.note: The fitted power law is reported for this motion-forecasting setup.
rows.check: Non-text setting. It bears on V3 only as a cross-domain allocation test and also on V5. The fit spans just over two orders of magnitude of compute.

rows.subject: Route-conditioned AV policies fine-tuned from the scaling series
rows.size_stated: Different model sizes; exact sizes not stated

rows.measure: Closed-loop failed scenarios versus pretraining compute
rows.value: Failures decrease with pretraining compute; the authors describe a similar scaling trend and a power-law decrease.
rows.note: The metric counts scenarios that fail any of the stated progress-mismatch or collision conditions; the figure includes an irreducible constant.
rows.check: Section 5.2 calls the decrease a power law. However, the Discussion says the compute range is too small to establish power laws for open- and closed-loop metrics. Each model's progress bias α was tuned per model.

rows.value: Models trained without AV show reasonable zero-shot generalization and follow a similar scaling trend as compute increases.
rows.note: The models used a different action-space configuration from the main scaling study.

rows.measure: Training miles needed to achieve matched AV cross-entropy loss
rows.value: Every 10 observed miles are equivalent to 2 to 3 demonstrated miles.
rows.note: The authors caution that all data came from the same AV-agent platform, so observed examples generally correlate with the AV ego-agent.
rows.check: This is an iso-loss data-equivalence ratio (10 observed miles ≈ 2–3 demonstrated miles), not a test of power-law form. It fits no version.

relationships.condition: Joint motion-forecasting cross-entropy, overall, per agent type, and zero-shot cross-agent transfer
relationships.reason: The compute-optimal loss fits a power law plus constant. Per-agent losses follow power laws with differing exponents, and AV-excluded training scales similarly (R1, R4–R7, R11). Allocation optima also follow power laws in compute (R2, R3).
relationships.display_finding: Compute-optimal loss follows a power law plus constant, agent-specific exponents differ, training excluding AV scales similarly, and optimal allocations follow compute power laws.
